paragraphs.text: FROM THE WORKS OF ORIGEN. “And it came to pass in the thirtieth year, in the fourth month, on the fifth day of the month, while I was in the midst of the captivity by the river Chebar, that the heavens were opened.” In many respects Ezekiel is a type of Christ, and you can begin to see this in the opening words of the prophecy: “It came to pass in the thirtieth year, in the fourth month,

on the fifth day of the month, and I,” he says, “was in the midst of the captivity by the river Chebar; and the heavens were opened.” These things have also been written about Christ: he was in this world, in this captivity, by the Jordan, when Jesus was beginning to be about thirty years old, and the heavens were opened to him. In the literal sense, the thirty years in the prophecy are the years of the prophet's life, while it was the fifth year of the captivity since they had gone down. His name too makes Ezekiel a symbol of Christ, for it means “strength of God.” And “son of man” points upward to the one who was called Son of Man. “I was in the midst of the captivity.” This is the sense the text bears. Put plainly, it means [?]: “I, who had no share in the captivity, was in the midst of the captivity for the sake of the divine plan.” So also Christ had not been taken captive, yet he was in the place of the captives for the sake of their redemption. In the same way the prophet was in the midst of the captivity not because of sins but to bring healing. “And I saw visions of God.” God has painted the invisible and intelligible nature in the visible and sensible nature, so that those who live by the senses may be trained by it toward contemplating the intelligible. “And the word of the Lord came to Ezekiel.” This is the Word who was in the beginning, the Word of God. Another comment: “I [said], ‘You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High.’” The Spirit calls gods those to whom the Word of God came, God the Word, for he is the one who makes people divine. “In the land of the Chaldeans.” “Chaldean” means “all toil.” These are astrologers who speak of fate. They are wholly fastened to the things of the senses and toil over them, making gods of them. The land of the Chaldeans is that place and that worst of conditions. Indeed, they are also a symbol of those who are arrogant in their impiety, the [?]

“And behold, a sweeping wind.” The spirit that sweeps away is God, for God is spirit, and he sweeps away wickedness. “And a great cloud.” This cloud is righteousness, the good that reaches us from God and enlightens us to the knowledge of the truth. “And brightness round about it.” “A likeness like the appearance of a man.” We are the likeness of the four living creatures. But ask what the three are. The charioteer of these four living creatures was not wholly fire. He was fire from the loins downward, and amber from the loins upward. For the Word has not only instruments of punishment but also means of giving rest. He punishes through the lower powers. The prophet did not see fire around the head, and the charioteer was not fire from the loins upward. He was fire from the loins downward, to show that those who live in the realm of birth are the ones who need fire, for the loins are a symbol of birth. And the words “from the loins downward” indicated not only those subject to birth

but also all who are below and passionately attached to matter, for birth and decay belong to matter. Amber is an alloy of gold and silver. These most precious things in matter are symbols of the precious, higher ranks of the holy powers.

“Son of man, stand on your feet.” As far as we remember, the address “Son of man” is used very often, throughout the whole prophecy, to Ezekiel, and more rarely to Daniel. Each of them, being in the captivity, is a type of Jesus the Savior, who came out to us captives.

“If perhaps they will hear, or take fright.” Similar to this expression of doubt is the one in Jeremiah: “Perhaps they will hear and repent.” In explaining that passage too we said that these things are said to encourage the hearers. Otherwise, on hearing what is said, they might think that, because our worse or better deeds have been grasped in advance by God's foreknowledge, it is impossible for the opposite of what was foreknown to happen. In fact, hearing and not hearing are equally in our power, just as if God had not foreknown. What is in our power is neither lessened because he foreknew nor would it be greater if he had not foreknown. By the same author. It would be safer to say “they will grow quiet” instead of “take fright.” Here, however, “take fright” is used of those who are moved by the divine oracles and progress from being alarmed at what is said to fearing God. And we must consider that “take fright” signifies something different here from what the Greeks mean by “fright,” which they define as a passion of the human soul. “And in it a roll of a book.” The divine words are partial and very small compared with the whole Word and all wisdom, and so they are called not a book but a kind of roll of a book. In the Psalms too the words “In the roll of the book it is written of me” show the same thing. But what lies at the right hand of the one seated on the throne is no longer called a roll of a book, but “a book written inside and on the back.” At any rate [?], John says, “No one in heaven or on earth or under the earth was able to open that book or to look into it,” except only the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, who has conquered. In the Revelation you will also find another written roll of a book, which John devours. For human nature cannot take in more than a roll to eat. “And there was written in it lamentation and song.” Song is for the saints, lamentation is for sinners who have not been given up on, and woe is for those being punished [?].

“And he fed me the roll.” This makes it especially clear that human nature cannot take in more than the roll to eat, even when it is fed by the hand of God. Yet the one who eats this roll will eat it when the hand stretched out toward him unrolls it. Through the unrolling of the roll he can grasp each of the things written in it. Having chewed the roll and its unrolling, he takes into his spiritual belly everything written on it, not only on the front but also on the back. I think the front of the roll indicates the principal doctrines: those about the saints and about the promises, and, in short, those about the blessed and the way they live. The back indicates what concerns those being punished and the manner of their punishment, and the things that followed in creation on what came first. The principal things on the front are indicated by the song, and the rest by the lamentation and the woe. I take it, then, that those who have fallen into sins and wholly fallen away from the doctrines of salvation are lamented. The song is proclaimed to the blessed, and the woe to those who have completely fallen away from blessedness. Someone who has tasted, in knowledge, the living bread that came down from heaven can also taste it in this way, when, after being lamented, he becomes worthy of blessedness. Theodotion translated in agreement with the Seventy. Symmachus, not very differently, has “laments and a recital, and a mournful song.” Aquila has “there was written on it creation and [?],” and “it will be.” Perhaps, according to him, this indicates that what was written concerned creation and, as it were, each person's portion. And it is clear that the good things contained in the promises, which will also come to pass, are signified by

“Not to a people deep of lip.” For if they were not people whose words are on the surface, and if their heart were their mouth because of the depth of their thoughts, you would not have gone to the house of Israel. “Nor are they heavy of tongue,” for their tongue, that is, their speech, has no weight and no elegance in its course [?]. They are light of tongue. Hence you must go to them, as they walk beneath your [?]. So “deep of lip” and “heavy of tongue” are said in praise. These things are said thus. And consider whether this is prophesied about those from the Gentiles, who are other than the house of Israel. The Hebrew prophet would not have understood them because of their foreign tongue. The same people can be called deep of lip because they do not grasp the divine writings superficially but believe their way into the depths of the law. “And hear with your ears.” For when a saint is plotted against and pursued by the opposing powers, he needs the Lord to cut the pursuers off from the pursued and, as it were, to guard the rear. A symbol of this is the passage in Exodus that reads: “[?] And the angel who went before the camp

of the sons of Israel moved and went behind them,” and so on. Consider also the voice heard behind him. Hearing a voice from behind may indicate knowledge of things already past. But if someone obtains divine grace to contemplate carefully the things to come as well, he would, as it were, hear a voice from in front of him. You will look for where this is said. “Blessed be the glory of the Lord from his place.” By the place of God we must understand all who have room for the power of God. But in the proper sense the place would be the Savior and Lord, just as the place of the Savior himself is the Father. In this way we have also understood the passage in Micah that reads: “For behold, the Lord goes forth from his place, and will come down and tread upon the heights of the earth,” and so on. For I think these words prophesy the descent of our Savior, who went forth from his place and came down from his former state with the Father. The place of God can, however, also mean what Paul calls unapproachable light, in the words “who alone has immortality, dwelling in unapproachable light.” What is this? It is the deepest knowledge of God, which no one can approach, nor can anyone have room to comprehend it. “I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel.” The saying “I have given you as a watchman to the house of Israel” is likely to be taken badly. So we needed to be taught how the prophet became a watchman. Then, when some people who have not paid attention to what is written leap upon the title of watchman, we can put them to shame from the whole passage by showing how one becomes a watchman and is given to the true sons of Israel. One becomes a watchman in this way: when, in addition to what was said before, the hand of the Lord comes upon someone. And it is not simply the hand of the Lord, but a strong hand. For perhaps the strong hand of the Lord does not come upon everyone on whom the hand of the Lord comes, since those counted worthy of the hand of the Lord are not even alike. One who enters the captivity must not enter it in a lowly way, suffering the same things as those taken captive. He must enter as one set apart and raised up, observing as if from a height the particular traits of each of those who have suffered the captivity and live by the streams of the river of the captivity, and the [?]

of the watchman. Thirdly, of the lawless man it is simply said: “The lawless man shall die in his lawlessness.” A trial is appointed for him: “For I will set the trial before his face,” he says. “And the hand of the Lord came upon me.” Those in the captivity could not hear him while he was standing, and so he sat in their midst. But when he is about to see the glory of the Lord, he rises and goes out into the plain, since only the breadth of the plain could hold the sight of the glory of the Lord that the prophet was about to see. “Go in and shut yourself in the midst of your house.” One who is still in the body cannot remain continually in the state of having gone out and standing. Bodily need calls him, even after divine contemplations, to enter the body again and, as it were, to undergo the condition of one shut in. For this reason, after he has seen the glory standing, and after he has been set upon his feet by the spirit, the words are spoken: “Go in, shut yourself in the midst of your house.” “Behold, bonds are laid upon you.” What else could the bonds laid upon the prophet be but the necessities of the body? Among these are the things that bind us, so that we cannot wholly escape them and get free of them. Because of them God binds our tongue to our throat, so that we do not share the fuller and most mystical teaching within us with those who embitter the Divine and have no room for words of reproof. Note, however, that where sins are more numerous, the prophet is commanded not even to reprove any longer, in the words “And you shall not be to them a man who reproves, for it is an embittering house.” Yet he is not commanded always to be silent and not to reprove. He is to reprove at the right time, because it is said: “And when I speak to you, I will open your mouth, and you shall say to them, ‘Thus says the Lord: Let the one who hears hear, and let the one who disobeys disobey.’”

“Take for yourself a brick.” I think the brick that is taken is each of those who, before they believe, are like a brick in mind. By the same author. I think the brick here means the soul of the uninstructed and foolish person. On it the city of Jerusalem is drawn by the prophet, and by anyone able to teach spiritual things and point out the better things, together with the mysteries in it and the account of the city of God and of those who have lived as its citizens. The siege works around the city would be doctrines that fortify the teachings about it, and the ramparts are the demonstrations that establish them. Perhaps also rational contemplation in itself, in whose knowledge the unassailable person must be, is signified by “And you shall cast a palisade around it.” The angelic guard is signified by “And you shall set camps against it.” And the siege engines around Jerusalem are the arguments that repel

opposing arguments. But since it is possible to sin even after so much, perhaps the words that take hold of the sinner and punish him are called an iron pan, just as, according to the prophet, a person is an iron wall because he does not fall away from the best disposition. “You shall set your face” means: you shall direct the discerning power of your soul toward the city, to build it on the brick, or else the city will be under siege. For you will enclose it by imprinting it on the soul of the hearer, who is clothed with a body, and shutting it in there. All this is laid down as a sign for those who exist in the realm of birth [?] and are called sons of Israel. Perhaps also, in those who have been taught the things of piety but do not live worthily of the holy teachings, the word is the city of Jerusalem drawn on the brick. It is surrounded and hemmed in by enemies who have ramparts and fence it with a palisade, setting their camps against it and countless siege engines to wound it. For this reason the iron pan is set up as an iron wall between the prophet and the besieged city, since the prophet is not like those people. The prophet's face is set toward the city on the brick, which is shut in under siege by the demonstration of the prophetic words. This too is all a sign to the sons of Israel, so that they may not become like this. “And you, take for yourself a pan.” The iron pan is probably the punishments. Or, according to the history, it refers to the barbarian's roasting the sons of the kingdom. “And you shall take the iniquities of the house of Israel.” The iniquities of the sons of Israel are two in number: that against God and that against rational beings. Who took them through his own lying down, if not our Savior? For those who had sinned more, he had to lie a longer time, not on the right and better side but on the left. For those who had transgressed less, he had to lie a shorter time on the right side. The text shows by this that the Savior suffered more for those who needed more healing. “And you, take for yourself wheat.” Someone may ask how our Lord, the Son of Man, eats such unclean bread among the nations. Let him understand that the Lord eats what people set before him, and they will see how no one can set clean bread before him. For he stands at the door and knocks, and if anyone opens to him, he comes in to him and dines with him. And I do not think it is clean food, but bread baked over [?] cow dung. But if we ever dine with him later, we will receive clean food from him in return for the food, not wholly unclean, that we set before him. And bonds have been laid on the Son of Man, who came into the midst of our captivity: material

and bodily bonds. For when he comes among us, he suffers with us and is bound together with us. He is with us in the exile of this life, hungering and thirsting with us. He eats with those who eat clean bread, and he drinks the water, but by weight and measure. For here he does not apportion to those he meets what they deserve. Because of our sins we ought to eat such bread baked on human dung. But to the extent that one may say with confidence, “My soul has not been defiled, and I have not eaten carrion,” and the rest, we are granted something of this kind. Our food is mixed with certain earthy, dung-like things, but not to such a degree, nor to excess, with unclean and foul-smelling things. I do not know which nourishments of the soul would be called wheat, which barley, which beans, and the rest. They are put into an earthenware vessel, that is, into the body taken and formed from the earth. He is commanded to eat twenty shekels. For bread so unclean, which was to be eaten, ought not to be received in a holy number, such as ten, seven, thirty, eight, or any similar number. It had to be received in the number twenty, which contains the dyad and division and is therefore akin to the unclean. This is clear from the unclean animals in the ark and from the animals Jacob sent to Esau, for most of them are sent to him in the number twenty. The number six is used for the measure of the drink, and the bread of wheat, barley, beans, and the rest is made from the number six. For this number is a symbol of the passion and affliction of the Savior, who suffered on the sixth day, and in the Revelation of John the name of the beast has the number 666. We are aware that some copies have 150 days, others 190 [?] days, and most 190 [?] days. But when we examined the other versions, we found that it is 390 days. All the things just described happen so that each of those who have done wrong may waste away in his iniquities and die because he is unjust. “Behold, I have given you cow dung.” So the prophet hints at something mystical about the soul taken captive, which cannot receive food wholly free from uncleanness. “Behold, I am breaking the staff of bread.” For this reason no whole, unbroken bread is found, and there is no staff of bread for the infants in captivity, for whom the bread must be broken.

“Thus says Adonai the Lord.” Where it concerns judgment, it was fitting [?] not to say, “There will be judgment in the midst,” but, “I will execute judgment in your midst.” And because they defiled the holy things of God, it says, “I too will reject you.” But where fathers ate sons, it does not say, “I will make fathers eat children or children eat their

fathers.” For the sons' being eaten on their account was not the fathers' sin. Nor is it fitting for God to bring such things about. This is also how the teacher of the Hebrews explained the words in First Kingdoms: “Those who glorify me I will glorify, and those who despise me shall be dishonored.” Glorifying had to be God's work. But that the one who dishonors God is dishonored is no longer God's doing; it is a consequence. This must also be observed in the blessings and curses in Leviticus and Deuteronomy, and in the prophetic words. What, then, is meant by “Therefore fathers shall eat their children in your midst, and children shall eat their fathers”? On a common and simpler interpretation, this can be seen in the unsettled and factious churches of

evildoers. Often those who taught others the divine law, and were thought to have begotten in Christ those who heard it from them, are plotted against by those they taught. They are then like fathers eaten by their sons. And if the teachers themselves exploit and wrong those they brought to the divine word, they are fathers eating their sons. That eating someone's flesh is used of such disorder and faction can be learned from Psalm 26: “When evildoers drew near to me to eat my flesh.” It can also be learned from Job, who says: “And if my maidservants have said, ‘Who would give us some of his flesh to eat, since he is so kind [?]’?” The Apostle says the same kind of thing when he rebukes those in certain churches who form factions against one another: “But if you bite and devour one another, take care that you are not consumed by one another.” This biting and devouring, which brings about “Fathers shall eat their children in your midst, and children shall eat their fathers,” is not God's doing. It is the consequence for those who reject God's ordinances and do not walk in his statutes. “And my wrath shall be brought to an end.” This shows that the wrath of God will have an end, like the consummation

By the same author. God's wrath is reproof, and his anger is discipline. And everyone who reproves and disciplines shows himself a father. By the same author. It is better to be disciplined by hearing of affliction than to experience [?] the actual work of discipline

What is said is announced to the mountains, but the prophecy concerns not only the mountains but also the hills, the glens and the ravines. For the hills, the ravines and the glens could not bear the fixed gaze of the prophet's face, and could not even receive what was said. These things are announced to the mountains, when they heard, because they deserved to suffer what was threatened, but not so that they would certainly suffer it. Those who hear, when hardships are impending, can change and so no longer fall into what they heard, as happened with the Ninevites. In Jeremiah too he says: “At length I will speak against nations and kings, to uproot and destroy them. And if they repent, I too will repent of all that I have spoken of doing to them.” The word is addressed to the mountains alone because they can take in the word about all; for none besides the mountains would grasp the intent of what is said. At the same time this text should be set before all who talk indiscriminately with anyone at all, and who share matters of greater weight with the simpler and most guileless. We must tell them that just as the prophet is ordered to speak what concerns mountains, hills, glens and ravines to the mountains alone, so ministers of the word are counselled to do the same. I take the mountains to be those naturally suited to sound knowledge. Those able to advance a little beyond others in knowledge are called hills. Those whose zeal is only for what must be done are called glens. Those whose souls are humbler than all are named ravines. “And your sacred precincts shall be taken away.” The word speaks to all who set out to examine the matters of knowledge and to live according to the law, but who can advance only a little in knowledge, or who seek nothing more than practice and are content with introductory teaching and small works: “Behold, I bring a sword upon you, and your high places shall be utterly destroyed.” For in such people one may find conceit, love of glory and a certain self-importance. It is good that puffing-up and conceit, which are the high places, be destroyed and wiped out. This rational sword will shatter whatever altars we build contrary to reason, thinking we owe God rational worship. These are the foundations we suppose we are building for the divine word, which the divine word now calls sacred precincts. “And by their eyes that go whoring.” To this we must apply: “Whoever looks at a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.” We must also apply what is found in Daniel about the lawless elders in the case of Susanna: “And the lawless men ordered her to be [uncovered?] (for she was veiled), so that they might be filled with her beauty.” And whoever has turned away from gazing on the beauty of the word of truth goes whoring with the eyes of the mind as well.

“Not in vain have I spoken.” I think the evils now spoken of, which are dealt out to those who deserve them for their correction, do not happen to no purpose, and that this is the meaning of “Not in vain have I spoken all these things to them.” Something is achieved when these things happen, for those who suffer them are helped and turn back. But if some persist in sin even after the punishments, the prophetic word says through Jeremiah: “In vain have I struck your children; you did not accept discipline.” It is likely that there too the children who are struck are the works of wickedness, since they are offspring of the wicked soul. Sometimes, when these are destroyed and struck, the wickedness remains no less; but often, when the works are hindered, the wickedness too is weakened. “Clap with your hand and stamp with your foot.” As far as the wording goes, the prophet is ordered, because of the multitude of the people's abominations, to show his indignation not only with his voice but also with a particular posture of the body. His hands are to clap in astonishment at the many sins, and his foot is to strike the ground hard enough to make a sound. Paraphrasing “And say, Well done!”, Symmachus has rendered: “I mourned and was indignant.” So we too must imitate the prophet. We must show indignation, vexed at sins, and disown them as in no way approving of what is done contrary to right reason. Perhaps too we clap with the hand by not cooperating with sinners, and we are said to stamp with the foot by not walking along with them. And we say “Well done!” in indignation when we assent to no abomination in word or deed.

“Thus says Adonai the Lord to the land of Israel.” Since the prophecy about the coming end is spoken to the land of Israel, I think that the wings of the land are those who are most discerning and soar on high beyond all who are on the earth. As to the body, they might in a way be said to be from the earth. The wings of the earth would be Israel, that is, those who have been taught to live according to the divine law. For from these wings of the earth we have heard wonders, as Isaiah says: “Lord, from the wings of the earth we have heard wonders.” Those who are, so to speak, the wingless of the earth do not know how to tell of wonders. For how are those not the wings of the earth whose nature is to grow wings like eagles? The four wings are said to be the four general orders into which the land is divided. First, surpassing all, is the house of Aaron; next to it, the house of Levi; third, Israel; and besides all these, as others distinct from them, those who fear the Lord. “The house of Israel hoped in the Lord; he is their helper and protector.” In another psalm the house of Levi is named besides these. The house of Aaron are the priests, and the house of Levi are, as one might say, those under

[?] the twelve tribes. Those who fear the Lord are people foreign to the seed of Israel who have attached themselves to the Lord, that is, proselytes. “And I will send upon you.” We should note that this is phrased paradoxically to convey a secret and most divine thought. “In your ways,” he says, “which are being punished, I will avenge you.” For when sinners are wronged, they have been wronged by no one other than themselves. Those who did wrong are punished as no other people than those who are avenged: the same people are both avenged and punished. So God, avenging those whom their own wickedness has wronged, punishes them insofar as they have done wrong. Through the punishment the wrongdoers are made to vanish, while the wronged are left, no longer having the wrongdoers within themselves; for they no longer have the wickedness that wronged them, nor its works. Pay attention also to “I will put upon you all your abominations.” He does not put some and leave others, but makes them all vanish. If one may say so, God puts all their abominations upon those who committed them even while benefiting them and showing them favour. This can be learned also from what is written in Amos: “You only have I known out of all the tribes of the earth; therefore I will avenge upon you all your sins.” There too the sense is something like this: “Since I have known you beyond all on earth, having chosen you as mine,” which agrees with “The Lord knew those who are his”, “therefore I will avenge upon you, as mine (whom I have known and whom I benefit), all your sins.” And like a good physician he says: “My eye shall not spare you, nor will I have mercy.” A physician who spares those who need deeper cutting and cautery, and pities them when they need greater torments and pains, applies a deficient treatment. That is what the one who says “My eye shall not spare you, nor will I have mercy” would have done, if he cared and pitied like a mere companion. So he will put each person's way upon him. The abominations of one who has sinned abominably will be in the midst of the sinner, perceived, as it were, and seen and condemned, so that afterwards those of whom the word speaks may know that he is the Lord, the Lord, and how he is Lord. Hosea too says: “I will avenge Jacob according to his ways, and according to his practices I will repay him.” There too the word shows the same thing by “I will avenge.” “One evil, evil, behold it is here.” The prophet foretells one evil, in which he says the end comes: the audacity of the Jews against Christ. By “the entanglement” he means the filling up of sins. It was for this reason that the Amorites were utterly destroyed, when their sins had been filled up. And when someone who sins much does not sin in some one matter, because he enjoys God's long-

suffering, and afterwards he too adds that sin to the sins he has already committed, it might fittingly be said of him: “One evil, evil, behold it is here; behold, the entanglement has come upon you.” “The rod has blossomed.” Perhaps, since God's benefits shine out after chastisements, the rod is said to blossom with the benefit that comes from the correction of the one being disciplined. In Isaiah too one of the prophecies about Christ runs thus: “And a rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall come up from the root.” I think the prophet also means this: by the rod, the saving word's power to rebuke and punish its hearers when they are reproved; by the flower, the result of the reproof and rebuke. So when any of us perceives that he is being struck by the divine rod, let him try to make the rod bring forth a flower, by enduring and accepting gladly what befalls him. See whether Aaron's rod can be a symbol of this. Long after he had held it, it sprouted and bore fruit. That was, as it were, a rod of God, as it is written: “And you shall take the rod which is from God.” Whoever carries it as one ought to carry God's rod will later see in it not only a flower but also fruit, so that it becomes worthy even to be laid up in the Holy of Holies in the [tent] of witness.

“For the vision is to the whole multitude.” For prophecy ceased after the Saviour's coming. And it is well said “to the whole multitude”, since there has come to be a remnant chosen by grace. “And a man in the eyes of his life.” If someone is holy, he will master what must be mastered. He will prevail by nothing other than the eye of his own life, which is the mind. In the mind we see the true life and overcome all who wrestle against us. “Blow the trumpet.” We have discussed the trumpet at greater length when examining “For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed.” To avoid repeating ourselves we will not dwell further on the passage, but only say this by way of reminder. Judging all things is greater than judging the twelve tribes of Israel, judging the angels or judging the world. These are spoken of in “You will sit on twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel”, in “We shall judge angels”, and in “By you the world is judged.” If so, we must train ourselves to blow the trumpet in order to judge all things. We must seek, then, the trumpet of God and the great voice of God that rouses God's soldiers to the contest against the enemy. The apostles were likely to have used such a voice when they so greatly roused people's minds, through the sound of the trumpet, to the contest against the foe. And since trumpets are also used at the feasts of God, as we have set out elsewhere,

these too must be taken up, so that through them we may urge the pure and true Israelites to keep the feasts of the Lord. So let each of us hear: “Lift up your voice with a trumpet”, and “Blow the trumpet at the new moon, on the notable day of your feast.” But let us not sound a trumpet before ourselves, as the hypocrites do; for it says, “Do not sound a trumpet before you.” Let us sound it rather before God, according to his spiritual law. Let us make for ourselves rational trumpets of beaten silver, in a settled disposition that produces divine utterances and words which teach how to wage war and how to keep festival, so that in this way we may be able to judge all things. “And baldness on every head.” Perhaps such a phrase is a symbol of mourning for sins. There are those who make themselves bald over the dead. In the same way, those who are ashamed of their own failings put off the adornment of their intellectual head, shave it, and bear on it the sign of mourning. But for the saints, who have nothing in common with enemies, the law laid down that they should not make themselves bald over the dead, “because,” it says, “you are holy to the Lord your God.” “And they shall enter them unguardedly.” We must consider the holy things to be defiled by those who defile the office of oversight and enter such things unguardedly. For example, we must say that someone enters the holy things of the church unguardedly if, after intercourse, he is indifferent to the impurity in himself and presumes to [?] the bread of the eucharist. Such a person profanes the holy things and causes confusion. “Woe upon woe.” First, woe in this life, by the very fact that he is wicked and impious and lacks God's oversight; second, woe in the punishments after this life. “And [threat?] shall be upon report.” Perhaps this means the preaching of the gospel, which came after the prophets who had threatened much about eternal punishment, and which plainly sets out what concerns Gehenna and the other unending torments. “And a vision will be sought.” Sometimes we read the prophetic words and the mysteries of the law without seeing what the prophets' visions are and what the law intends. This happens because those who boast of God's priesthood not only break the law but also destroy its true sense. Then will be fulfilled: “A vision will be sought from a prophet.” But we must be quick to find the vision sought from the prophet. And if the law has at some time perished from a priest, the priest seeks somehow to find it again by understanding and doing the law, so that he may also guide others by the hand to keep it. And when people preside who are not fit to give counsel or to consider what the common good requires, we must say that counsel has perished from the elders. “And the ruler shall clothe himself with destruction”: he will, if he does not put on Christ Jesus, the breastplate of righteousness and the whole armour of God, so as to be able to stand against the wiles of the devil. For every ruler who sins will clothe himself with destruction. And the hands of the people grow feeble when the way of life of the

people is watery, disorderly and slack. But when it makes use of the strength of God, it [ceases?] to be a people of the land and becomes a people of heaven, seeking the kingdom of heaven. “And counsel from the elders.” Not even human counsel will benefit them, he says, nor will they have any useful advice. “The king shall mourn, and the ruler.” “The king shall mourn” is commonly [marked with an asterisk?]. Perhaps this is because of the Saviour, who would not be thought to mourn, so that the Seventy did not translate the phrase; or perhaps they had not then found the words in the Hebrew. Yet it is not absurd, keeping the text, to say that the king too mourns, since the Saviour wept over Jerusalem. “And in their judgments I will avenge them.” God judges the one who has offended by the judgments of the one who sinned. That is so if it is true that “As you judge, you will be judged”, and “In whatever judgment you judge another, you condemn yourself; for you do the same things.”

“And the hand of the Lord came upon me.” In some copies it is written, “the hand of the Lord Lord.” We have said elsewhere that in many places what is expressed by the word “Lord” is, among the Hebrews, the venerable name of God, which they do not readily utter. Yet sometimes “lord” is also used of a master of servants. So where “Lord Lord” stands, one must know that one of the two is, as it were, the proper and unutterable name of God. The other “Lord”, Adonai for the Hebrews, they apply to the Lord. Sometimes they pronounce this word in place of the unutterable name, and sometimes they use it as of a master of servants. So for one who has understood what was said about the unutterable name, “Adonai Lord” differs in no way from “Lord”, as we have explained. “And he took me by the crown of my head.” There are several inner gates as well, one facing south, another east and another west. But he is led to the one facing north, so that, looking up from there, he may see the [punishments?] brought upon those who sin in this northern world. For there are other worlds on the earth too, as the sciences also show. Clement says: “The Ocean, impassable to men, and the worlds beyond it are governed by the same [?] ordinances of the Master.” And since the sins of those in the northern world just mentioned are many, there stands at the entrance of the former gate, the one facing north, the pillar of the image of jealousy. It is the jealousy of him who says, “I am a jealous God.” Through this jealousy he makes his own those whom wickedness has most estranged, acquiring them for himself. Among human beings, then, it is not the archetypal jealousy but an image of jealousy that is at [work?]. “See the wicked lawless deeds that they are doing

[?] here.” Sinful elders make idols. Within themselves they fashion every likeness of reptile through the venom of wickedness, and every likeness of beast through unbridled desire. And if they hold false opinions about divine things, they fashion vain abominations; for every falsehood about divine things is impious and is therefore also a vain abomination. There are some whose walls, so to speak, of the house of the soul are painted all over with every likeness of reptile and beast and with vain abominations. They serve these, sacrifice to them as to gods and burn incense to them, so that the vapour of the incense rises. That is, the admiration for these things is exalted and lifted up by them. They inscribe these things all around on their minds, leaving no place in them empty of evils, so that the whole is written over with evils. They have even transferred the sacred cycle of the seven from holy things to idols, so that they take on, as it were, a fixed stability in what is worse. Such is the meaning of “And seventy men of the elders of the house of Israel.” When the prophet's mind, led in by the Spirit, sees what is in the house of each sinner's soul, it looks at the entrance of the court. There is a hole, a trace, in what is called the wall. When this hole is examined further and dug out by the searching word, one who has been enlightened by the divine Spirit can see everything. Beyond the hole he sees a door as well, through which he can also pass, understood in a spiritual sense. The Saviour also speaks of this door in the Revelation of John, a door found in each [?] person: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock; if anyone opens to me, I will come in to him and dine with him.” “Because they said: The Lord has forsaken.” What was seen never concerned some one appointed place, but each person's chamber, and the hidden chamber at that. For Scripture customarily calls what belongs to the ruling faculty of the soul “hidden”, and sometimes also an “inner room.” Such is the meaning of “Go into your inner room”, and “He who sees in secret will reward you.” Not far from these is what is called the hidden man of the heart. It is more plausible that sinners suppose, concerning this hidden place too, that the Lord, though he sees, does not see them. “The Lord has forsaken the land” can also be said by those who think that divine providence does not reach the earth and what is in it. For there are some who did not take providence away from heavenly and ethereal things, being abashed by the order found there. But they stripped it, together with [the divine] power, from the earth, saying, “The Lord has forsaken the

“Weeping for Tammuz.” The figure the Greeks call Adonis, they say, is called Tammuz among the Hebrews and Syrians. So, as the wording goes, the women were seen sitting at the entrance of the gate of the house of the Lord that faces north, and according to some [heathen custom?] [?] Ezek. 8:12. Matt. 6:6.

[?] …custom of those outside the doors of godliness: weeping for Tammuz. For they are thought to hold certain rites every year: first, they weep for him as dead; second, they rejoice over him as risen from the dead. Those who are skilled in the allegorical interpretation of Greek myths and of what is considered mythical theology say that Adonis is a symbol of the fruits of the earth. These are mourned when they are sown, but they rise again and so make the farmers rejoice when they spring up. I think, then, that the women weeping for Tammuz are a symbol of those who long for what are considered the goods of the world and for bodily fruits, and who know nothing beyond material and sensible things. Such people grieve when they are deprived of these things and take pleasure in having them and acquiring them. All such people might reasonably be thought to have effeminate souls. "My eye will not spare." We must examine what "My eye will not spare" means, for it does not say, "I will not spare." I think, then, that God's power of sight, as though it fixed its gaze on those whose intellect has been defiled by an evil conscience, punishes them, since "our God is a consuming fire", consuming, clearly, whatever has taken on wickedness. And when he does these things, he does not act sparingly against what is worse, in that he does not spare those to whom such things have happened. "Nor will I have pity." This shows that the pity spoken of here is pity understood in a bad sense [?]. Those skilled in these matters have defined this pity as grief at a neighbour's misfortune. They say that a physician or a judge ought not to feel this kind of pity. Otherwise, confused by the grief that leads to pity of this kind, they may be hindered from carrying out their medical or judicial work for the good of the patient or of the person on trial.

"And a sapphire girdle on his loins." Instead of "a sapphire girdle on his loins", Aquila and Theodotion have put "a scribe's kasto", keeping, I think, the Hebrew word. For I do not think that among the Greeks the word kasto means having a writer's tablet on one's loins. But one of the Hebrews said that it is what is called a kalamarion, that is, a pen case, and that this is the kasto. "And give a mark." The Seventy say that the one clothed in the long robe was commanded by the glory of the Lord to put a mark on the foreheads of those who groan and are in pain. Aquila and Theodotion say, "the marking of the Tau upon the foreheads of those who groan and are in anguish." When we asked the Hebrews whether they had any ancestral teaching to tell us about the Tau, we heard the following. One said that the Tau is the last of the twenty-two letters of the Hebrews in their order of the alphabet. So the last letter was taken to represent the per-

-fection of those who, because of the virtue in them, groan and are in anguish over the sins committed among the people, and who suffer along with the transgressors. A second said that the Tau is a symbol of those who have kept the Law. Among the Hebrews the Law is called Torah, and its first letter is Tau, so the Tau is a symbol of those who have lived according to the Law. A third, who said he was one of those who had believed in Christ, said that in the ancient script the Tau looks like the shape of the cross. He said it is a prophecy of the sign that Christians make on the forehead, which all believers make before beginning any undertaking whatever, and especially prayers or holy readings. "For the land was filled with many peoples." Instead of "peoples", the others have rendered "blood". With them the meaning is clear: all those who sin unto death are full of blood, because of the multitude of those who sin unto death. But if we follow the Seventy's reading, "the land was filled with peoples", it will mean that the many foreign doctrines, alien to the Godhead, that arise in us are not one people but many discordant peoples. Or perhaps the sins are these: the land, which is distinct from the city and ought to be full of fruits, is empty of them, and instead holds peoples who are abandoning the city, or the cities [?]. The injustice of the nation of Israel and Judah has been magnified exceedingly, because the city has been filled with injustice and uncleanness. We too have within ourselves both a land that must be farmed and a city that must be built, if indeed we are "God's field, God's building". Those who do not tend these, but have only peoples and injustice, are those whose injustice alone has been magnified exceedingly. Those whose injustice has not yet been so magnified are still lacking something before it is [?]. The same holds for uncleanness. The cause of these things, however, is the supposition that Providence does not reach the things on earth. For they say, "The Lord has forsaken the land; the Lord does not see."

"The likeness of a throne above them." The prophet sees not a throne but the likeness of a throne. In the same way, he says earlier that he saw not the glory of the Lord but the likeness of the glory of the Lord: "This was the vision of the likeness of the glory of the Lord." And it is no wonder if those who cannot yet perceive things face to face see likenesses of all those things when they are found worthy to behold them. I think too that when Daniel saw dreams about the kingdoms up to the consummation and the resurrection, he was in a vision in which likenesses were shown to him. So when someone sees in a waking state, with his ruling faculty impressed by the prophetic Spirit, he pictures certain likenesses that symbolize the true realities. For the soul is mingled with a thick and earthy body, and this does not allow it to behold anything more distinctly [?] and more clearly.

Note now that the man was clothed not in a long robe but in a garment. He was about to hear, "Go in between the wheels beneath the cherubim, and fill your hands with coals of fire." So he had to be dressed more brightly, since he was about to purge the city which, as he said before this, had been filled with men.

"Who say: Have not the houses been newly built?" The sense of the passage is this. These people, he says, see that the city has recently been rebuilt after the earlier captivity, and they say: "Even if the houses have been newly built, this city is like a cauldron full of dead bodies held inside it. We are like the meat in the cauldron, with the fire of the Babylonians all around us, so that we cannot escape the flame of the enemy's fire." But what you have said is not true, he says. You spoke truly when you said that the city is a great cauldron, but not when you said that you are the meat in its midst. For the dead whom you struck down in its midst are the meat, and the city is the cauldron. You will not remain in the city, for I will drive you out. So if the city is a cauldron for others, it is not one for you; and if some will be meat in its midst, it will not be you. For I will judge you when you have come to the very borders of the mountains of Israel. I will bring all these things upon you, so that afterwards you may recognize that I am the Lord.

"Prophesy against the prophets of Israel." Prophets are those who serve the word of teaching well and prophesy the things of God. "And you shall say to the prophets who prophesy from their own heart." False prophets are those who give out oracles from their own worthless heart, and whatever the opposing power dictates to them. By the same. Whatever is recorded about prophets or false prophets applies to all teachers and false teachers, visible and invisible. By the same. Whoever speaks from his own heart, apart from the divine Spirit, is a false prophet. "Woe to those who prophesy from their own heart." Whoever walks after his own spirit follows the wishes of the soul. Whoever walks after the Holy Spirit walks after the Lord God and does his will. By the same. The Apostle says to those who walk after their own spirit, "I will pray with the spirit, I will pray with the mind." And you will ask whether the two are one or not, and what they are. "Your prophets, Israel, are like foxes." This kind, or rather this animal, is crafty, beastly and wild. It is taken to stand not only for the wicked, crafty and deceitful person but also for spirits of the same sort. For these too work their own designs

in the soul that has become a desert, abandoned by God and his righteousness. Look into the behaviour of the animal as well. "They did not stand on a firm foundation." By this he hinted at what is unstable, false and powerless. "And they gathered the flocks." That is, the heretics against the Church, the brutish doctrines against the truth. "They did not rise up in battle." They did not rise with Christ, because they were not buried with him: those who speak of and see a false day of the Lord. "Have you not seen a false vision?" A false vision means doctrines conceived falsely. "They shall not be in the instruction of my people." The Lord's chastenings are of different kinds. There is a chastening that is said to be in judgment, and there is a chastening that is said to be in wrath. "Nor shall they be written in the register of the house of Israel." For they will be blotted out of the book of the living. "And they shall not enter the land of Israel." In the day to come, that is. "Therefore you shall not see false things." That is, I will not let you prosper, so that what follows may be fulfilled [?]. CHAPTER 14. "If I answer them in reply." "If I answer them in reply": God takes judgment from you, that is, from the prophet. Or else it clearly means that he answers such people themselves. So, prevailing over judgment, he promises to answer them as one who is merciful. "Whoever sets his thoughts." Here he teaches how one should answer each person with a reply that suits him, and not at random. He also teaches that it is the Lord himself who answers through the prophet. "I the Lord will answer him in the things in which his heart is entangled." That is, the things it follows, delights in and clings to. Such things give the slack and faint-hearted a pretext for turning aside from God. Even so, though they are such people and their heart clings to such things, since they wanted to inquire of the Lord, he answers them through the prophet as people who need to turn back, saying, "Turn back and turn away," and so on.

"A land, if it sins." Divine Scripture often names the dwelling or the condition in place of those who live there, and again those who live there in place of the dwelling. So in "if the land sins", it has named earthly people by the word "land". For this reason man and beast will be destroyed from it. Another interpretation: if the earthly disposition sins (for it is its nature to sin), man and beast will be destroyed from it, that is, the brutish man and the more rational man. For it cannot be said that this earth we tread on is rational and itself sins, as some have imagined. For if we grant this,

[?] we will have to say that all things have souls, and side with those who teach the transmigration of souls. "And I will break its staff of bread." That is: they will be punished in proportion to their injustice. By the same. When our land sins, the outer man is punished by a sensible famine, and the inner man is punished by an intelligible famine, the loss of spiritual bread. Both the outer and the inner man suffer anguish; and whatever the outer man suffers in the realm of the senses, the inner man suffers just as much in the realm of the intellect. By the same. The soul of each of us is also called land. One land has a paradise, another has thorns; one is called good, another evil. The Lord's parable shows this. "And if these three men are in its midst, Noah, Job and Daniel." These saints are taken as types. Take anyone who does not corrupt his way of life on earth. He does not become wholly flesh by following the mind of the flesh, so as to be called entirely flesh. Instead he shines like a light in the world, holding out the word of life in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation, so that God himself declares to him, "I have seen you alone righteous in this generation." Everyone of this kind is Noah, and what is recorded of Noah applies to him as well. For the two have become equal in their condition, so that both are called Noah. By the same. Take anyone who resolves in his heart not to defile himself with the food and drink of the intelligible Nebuchadnezzar, but to afflict his soul with fasting in this Babylon for the sake of the knowledge of the truth. Such a person is Daniel, and what is recorded of Daniel can fittingly be said of him too. For their condition is one and their disposition the same, so that both are called Daniel. By the same. Take anyone who is blameless in life and true in godliness, keeping away from all evil, so that the devil grows jealous of him and brings every kind of temptation upon him in his trials, and yet he does not give way even in a word of his lips. Such a person is Job, and what is recorded of Job will fit him too. For both are equal, sharing one disposition in the Lord, and both will be called Job. "If sons and daughters shall be saved." Daniel has sons by a spiritual generation, whom his prophecy begot. He had no sons in the flesh, for he was a eunuch, as they say. And this is clear, for it was by these [?] that he was handed over to the chief eunuch. If, then, these three men, Noah, Job and Daniel, are found in the land that has sinned, they will be saved by their righteousness. It is as if he said: even if men like Noah, Job and Daniel are found there. "If sons and daughters shall be left." That is, they will not be left. "They alone, Noah, Daniel and Job, [will save] their souls by their righteousness", that is, only their own. For there is

elsewhere in the divinely inspired Scripture an expression of this kind that carries an evident negation. An example is what Elijah said to Ahab: "As the Lord God of hosts lives, the God of Israel, before whom I stand, if there shall be dew or rain on all the earth in these years." So too the Lord in the Gospel according to Mark: "This generation seeks a sign. Truly, truly I say to you, if a sign shall be given to this generation", that is, it will not be given. The saying in the Psalms is like these: "As I swore in my wrath, if they shall enter my rest." It is said in place of "they shall not enter." [?] "…bring out sons and daughters." This is to be read as a question. If, he says, Noah, Daniel and Job will not be enough to save those threatened with a single punishment, will they be able to bring their sons and daughters out of destruction when all four punishments are brought upon them? "Behold, they will come out to you", you who were taken captive earlier. Comparing yourselves with the evils that have come upon them, you will be comforted, because you have suffered far less.

"Among the trees of the forest." The "trees of the forest" there must be understood as the wild trees, the pine and the like. By this he means to compare Israel with the other nations, as a vine that has enjoyed cultivation. It had the Law, priests, the promise given through the prophets, a holy temple, and many wonders: fire that came of itself and consumed the sacrifices, a voice that came from the mercy seat of the cherubim, and other things like these. "They will come out of the fire." When they are called back from Nebuchadnezzar's captivity, another captivity will take them, that of Vespasian, carried out through Titus. He is pointing to the unbroken succession of their calamities.

"And they did not bind your breasts." Whoever is at the first stage of contemplation does not suck outside wisdom but is nourished from it within. So some have rightly said that the two breasts are the two Testaments, at which the infants suck. These sucklings are the ones out of whom the Lord has perfected praise, to destroy the enemy and avenger. "Nor did your eye spare." That is, you had no compassion on yourself and did not spare yourself enough to do even one of the things mentioned before, so as to move me too to compassion. "And I passed by you." God is impassible, just as he is unchangeable and uncreated. But his acts of providence vary according to the variety of the things he governs, for he is the maker of all. So some of his dispensations are wrathful and others jealous. In the same way, for his spiritual servants there are dispensations of grace, glory and exultation, all from the one God who is unchangeable, impassible and almighty.

By the same. God suffers with us in showing mercy, for God is not without compassion. "And I washed you in water." With the washing and grace of the Holy Spirit, and with the sanctifying word. "And I anointed you with oil." The anointing is the indwelling of the Holy Spirit in the knowledge of the truth. "And I clothed you in embroidered garments." The embroidered garment is the disposition adorned with many different virtues, formed from true doctrines and pious practice. "And I shod you with hyacinth." He adorned the soul's movement with pure hyacinth, stripping away the deadness that had been brought into it. It is also of the whole life

By the same. These things can also be applied to the soul. The sandal means works that go forward unhindered. The girdle means keeping the counsels of the mind secure. The cloak means standing on the truth while bowing down [?]. The bracelets mean doing nothing improper. The necklace means boldness for the good. The pendants mean ready obedience to the Law. The crown of boasting means the promise of God, which he has set apart for those who do right. "And I girded you with fine linen." Fine linen is surely a symbol of truth and of true chastity. It means: I made you my own, and did not let you go about shamefully ungirded like some common woman [?]. By the same. The cloak there is the half-cloak. The hair-net there is the one made of gold. By the same. God puts bracelets on the hands of the soul. They are the occasions for good deeds, and also the deeds themselves, done by the power of the Holy Spirit. For bracelets are a symbol of action. By the same. The ring at the nostril is the true knowledge of the mysteries, which is most fragrant. By the same. The pendants at the ear, like a great golden earring, are the divine oracles, from which the mind builds up for itself the knowledge of the truth. By the same. The crown of boasting is blameless work, made perfect by true doctrines. By the same. The adornment of gold and silver is the adornment formed in the ruling faculty from divine thoughts and sacred words. By the same. The hair-nets are, as if he said, very fine thoughts, deep thoughts, or varied thoughts, because of the different kinds of virtue. "And the incense." Incense and oil are the prayer sent up to God from the mind with knowledge, in which God shares the delight. "And you spread your legs on every byway." By the leg he hinted at the movement of the mind, by which it went toward every byway. A byway is anything that does not travel along the truth. For the Truth said, "I am the way." So everything conceived in opposition to it is called a byway. "And you played the harlot three times over." That is, in many ways.

For the three tenses are taken to cover all ages. "Sodom your sister." Sodom is a symbol of practical wickedness, that is, sin committed through the flesh. "She and her daughters." The daughters of Sodom are souls that have not learned that "everyone who exalts himself will be humbled." By her daughters he means the other cities. Note in Scripture the difference between sins, small and great. The extreme of wickedness is pride, the passion of the author of evil, into which the Sodomites too appear to have fallen. Look into this as well.

"Say now to the rebellious house of Israel." Rebellion is sin, for its Greek name comes from "bitter", and painful things are called bitter. "Against Jerusalem." Jerusalem is a symbol of knowledge, of the holy Church and of virtue; the three are aspects of one thing. Whoever is in Jerusalem and gives himself over to sin has given room to the devil, the intelligible Nebuchadnezzar, to come against him. The devil then pulls down the wall around Jerusalem, which is the discipline of self-control, through the chief cook, which is the intemperate life. And he will carry off a complete captivity from Jerusalem, that is, from virtue, to Babylon, and [?] "And I will bring him in under a curse." When the devil brings people into his covenant, he brings them in under a curse; for he calls the covenant and the oath a curse. "Who dishonoured my curse." A person dishonours God's curse when he does not endure the chastening to which God hands him over, but turns instead to the rest that sin offers. Therefore such a person will not escape. "And I will take from the choice ones." "And after these things I will take from the choice parts of the cedar." What is set out here will happen after those handed over to chastening have been chastened. According to the letter, he is prophesying the return of that people. The choice parts of the cedar are the apostles and those like them, the seed according to election. According to the anagogical sense, they are the disposition renewed through chastening, a good nature

"I will plant it on a high mountain." The high mountain is the knowledge of the truth, Christ. "And I will hang it on a lofty mountain." The lofty mountain is the heavenly place, and the disposition that corresponds to it. "And it will become a great cedar." He means the Church and the word within it, under which the unclean birds and the unclean winged creatures will one day find rest. By the same. Whoever has been given wings by the words of God will rest under the great cedar that God planted on the high mountain. [?]
"And its branches will be restored." They will be restored in Christ. In him will rest the [?]

"And all the trees of the plain shall know that I am the Lord." A tree is a rational nature; the plain is either the breadth of reasonings or the lower regions. "Who brings low the high tree." The high tree is the people that was once exalted in virtue, but was also exalted in wickedness, and for this it was brought low. "And who exalts the low tree." The low tree, growing close to the ground, is the people of the Gentiles: low in sins, and low because it began from below, as it were from childhood; it will be exalted to the summit, as it is written: "The last shall be first." "And who dries up the green tree." The green tree is the one that lives a life of righteousness. The dry tree is the one that lives a life of sin, and this is why it is dried up. By the same author. For the intelligible tree is a rational nature that has started from the middle and does not yet live in righteousness.

"The fathers have eaten sour grapes." In these words he teaches that what is said in the laws of Israel, that the sin of the fathers is repaid upon the children, is a parable that requires insight. By the same author. The sour grape is lawless sin. It is called a sour grape because it takes its starting points from our natural impulses. Just as the sour grape grows naturally from the vine, so we too are eating sour grapes if in our early years we follow wherever our natural impulses draw us. By the same author. The sour grape is sin. The setting of the teeth on edge is the deadness that sin brings about in us, and the teeth are the power of the soul. "If this parable shall still be spoken." Parables are not to be understood according to the literal facts but according to the higher sense. The law that said that the sins of the fathers are repaid upon the children also said that sons shall not die for their fathers. For one person cannot receive the recompense due to another, a father for a son or the reverse.

"The soul that sins, it shall die." He means the death that comes from sin, through being deprived of the one who said: "I am the life [?]." "The man who shall be righteous." A righteous man is one who does judgment: who does nothing without judgment but everything with judgment, in righteousness. "He shall not eat upon the mountains." He means that food of the heights that exalt themselves against the knowledge of God. These mountains are intelligible ones, ranged on the side of the adversaries, those who begot them [?]. "To the idols of the house of Israel." By idols he means the passions as they exist in the mind. "To a woman in her separation." He means the days of purification. By this he gradually trains us toward the highest chastity.

"He will not give his money at interest." "Interest" is the term for what is given on money; "increase" is what is given on other things, such as food or drink. The pestilent man is one who does harm: the robber, the unjust man, the one who swallows up everything. "And sheds blood." Blood is a symbol of the soul's life-giving power. "And the poor and needy." The pestilent man cannot oppress the rich, for "a man's own wealth is the ransom of his soul, but the poor man cannot stand up to threats." Rich is the one who is rich in good works, in the word of God, and in all knowledge. "And has set his eyes on idols." Everything fabricated is an idol, and the heretics set these up in secret. "But if he begets a son." Our birth is according to the flesh, and it is through this birth that we have fathers and mothers. The soul has no mother or father, for God alone is its maker and father. Teaching this, God says: "All souls are mine." Each soul has its own existence and stands on its own account, not on another's. So no one can say that one soul pays the penalty for the sins of another. "In his transgression which he transgressed." He calls all transgressions one transgression, and again the one is pictured by the many. That people committed a transgression when they killed our Lord Jesus Christ. Each person transgresses when he loses reason and falls into unreason. "The way of the Lord is not right." Israel says this when they see the Gentiles entering in. "Is it not your way that is not right?" It depends on you. "Cast away your impieties from yourselves. And make for yourselves a new heart." And how will this happen? It will happen if we strip off the old man with his deeds and put on the new man, who is being renewed in knowledge after the image of the one who created him. It will happen when we go up from earthly things into the great upper room, swept clean of all wickedness, adorned and furnished with perfect virtue, and keep the feast with Jesus. There we take the cup of the new covenant and form the likeness of his body in our mortal body by sharing in him.

"Why is your mother a whelp living among lions?" This is taken figuratively: a rational being becomes a lion, or any other beast, by its habits, and likewise every animal and creeping thing. By the same author. By the lion's mother he was hinting at the synagogue of the ruler of Israel. It too became like a wild beast in many things, and above all when it raised its voice against its Master, saying: "Away with him, away with him, crucify him!" By the same author. Many people differ in no way

from beasts; or rather, they are worse than beasts in their savagery and inhumanity. Such was this man who is called the ruler of Israel. "And he laid waste the land and its fullness with the sound of his roaring." This second lion was not only a lion that destroyed men by his impious deeds. He is also a symbol of those who lay waste the earth and its inhabitants with their most impious doctrines. So in the literal sense these lions are symbols of the kings of Jerusalem: the first was handed over to Egypt, and the second, being more impious, to Babylon. But the passage also has a higher sense for those able to contemplate it. The impious heretics, who do not keep the word but trample on it, suffer such things too. Some are handed over here to the intelligible Egyptians; others, either here or after their departure from this life, to the intelligible Nebuchadnezzar.

"And I gave them statutes that were not good." What were these but the killing letter of the law, the covenant of death engraved in letters on stone, and the ministry of condemnation? Both the letter and the spirit are commanded by the same voice. But the commands according to the letter are not to be done, while those according to the spirit are to be done. Such conduct is blameless even when it profanes some of the commandments. We learn this not only from the Apostle of the new covenant; it is clear also from the times before the Saviour's coming. The priests in the temple profane the Sabbath and are guiltless. A man is circumcised on the Sabbath, so that one law is broken and another kept. David and those with him ate of the loaves of presentation, which it was not lawful for him or his companions to eat, but only for the priests. Likenesses of the cherubim were made both in the tent of witness and in the temple. And Moses fashioned the likeness of a bronze serpent.

"Behold, the house of Israel have all become mixed for me." The Lord sits in the midst of Jerusalem, smelting those who are mixed with silver and tin, bronze and lead. He accuses those who carry worthless material about them and says: "They have become alloyed silver." For when we bring worthless things from our own wickedness into the good creation of God, we bring in lead, bronze and tin: evil deeds, godless doctrines, and attachment to the body. It is because of these that the fire is needed.
"You have put on every precious stone." The high priest wore twelve stones on his shoulders, which adorned him for his service as high priest to God. These stones the virtuous man builds

upon the unshakable foundation, and fire cannot burn them up. He builds them on his own shoulders, that is, by his own labors. In the midst of them, the one who possesses them wears on his breast the precious stone of manifestation and truth. The twelve stones are the principles of the sons of Israel, and in these stones you will contemplate the intelligible trees of paradise. Among them is the tree of life: whoever has gained it will have his head crowned [?] with the holy plate of the Lord. The gates of Jerusalem were made of such holy stones, and so was the whole of Jerusalem. The ruler of Tyre had once put all of them on, not by his own labors but by grace, as the principle of Jerusalem and as a priest of God. But he fell from all of them, because he said in his heart: "I am God; I have dwelt in the dwelling of God in the heart of the sea." The heart of the sea is the deep principles of the deeps, the innermost of the innermost. The one who was exalted by this fell from that heart and was cast down into the visible sea itself. The same thing happens to people who are exalted by their own labors. "You are a seal of likeness." Truth is a seal and a crown of beauty. Whoever is in the truth will be shaped by it, and those who receive the truth come to be in it. "Because of the multitude of your sins I have cast you down to the earth." The one who was cast down to the earth was cast from the heavens, whose copy and shadow those who served in the tabernacle served. "Set your face firmly." Divine Scripture narrates what has happened among us human beings, and so teaches us in matters that concern us. From those matters it guides the one who follows it, leads him upward, and shows him the intelligible through the sensible. From what has happened among us, it points out to the spirit what happened among those who were before us; I mean those outside the flesh. For the narrative has its own sense, namely what happened among us human beings, but it also has a corresponding higher sense concerning those who were before us.

"Behold, I am against you, Pharaoh, king of Egypt." Pharaoh was indeed a real man, king of this Egypt by the river Nile, who oppressed the sons of Israel at that time and drowned their infants. But he also stood for the devil. Every king in the narrative who is like him stands for some devilish and apostate power. This is shown by the words: "Behold, I am against you, the great dragon that sits in the midst of the river of Egypt," and what follows. It does not make sense to say these things in the literal sense of a man. "Who says: The rivers are mine." He not only says, "The rivers are mine, and I made them," but also that he sits as lord [?] in the midst of his rivers. These come from the belly of those who conceived

them, and they are powerful in falsehood; those who drink from them go out to eternal death. So that they may not be drunk, God turns them into blood, and it is not written that he turned them back into water. "And I will put a snare in your jaws." God puts snares in the dragon's jaws to muzzle his mouth, put an end to impious teaching, and bring him up out of the water onto dry land. "And I will make the fish of your river stick to you." The fish of the river of Egypt are those who seem to live their lives in Egyptian, bodily passions. These stick to the dragon's fins and scales, tossed and carried about by every wind of teaching through human trickery. By the same author. The fish clinging to the fins of the intelligible Pharaoh, who is in the midst of the rivers of wickedness, are those who become disciples of wickedness. They drink the Egyptian water, are united with the dragon in the watery condition, and come under his authority. "Because you have been a staff of reed." A person may refuse to lean on the rod from the root of Jesse. He may not be disciplined by the rod with which God punishes the lawlessness of the sons of David, nor admonished by the apostolic rod. If he leans instead on false and empty words, he leans on a staff of reed, the dragon Pharaoh. "And I will destroy man and beast from you." Just as God has men and beasts whom he saves, so too does the dragon Pharaoh. God destroys them, not simply, but from the dragon. Or perhaps these are the very ones who receive this salvation, since they no longer belong in any way to the dragon Pharaoh.

"It shall be the end of the nations." The end of the nations is the hand of the Lord upon all Egypt and Ethiopia. What concerns human beings is said of the Egyptians, and what concerns the opposing powers is said of the Ethiopians. "And the sword shall come upon the Egyptians." In many places Egypt is understood as this world, the human [?] and earthly one, from which the true Israelites go out and journey toward the holy

"And its foundations shall fall." Because God is good, he overturns the foundations of Egypt, so that no Egyptian building may remain; I mean sin. For the Word uproots, demolishes and destroys wickedness, and builds up virtue. "Persians and Cretans and Lydians and Libyans, and all the mixed peoples of the sons of my covenant shall fall by the sword." Who can describe each of these nations and interpret each of them, in the way required, as

wicked? It belongs to God, and to God alone, to give the true account of all these things. When you search for the meaning that lies in Scripture, ask God for illumination. "From Migdol to Syene they shall fall by the sword." Migdol is where Egypt begins on this side; Syene is the farthest part of Egypt, right next to the Ethiopians. The Egyptians are a symbol of people who live in sins. Egypt is the world that lies in the power of the evil one, or the condition of wickedness. Syene and Migdol are the borders of Egypt. So those in Syene are the people who are at the beginning of wickedness, at its entrance, as it were. Even so, all the Egyptians must be punished, from the first to the last. All who dwell in Egypt, or rather who are Egypt, will be punished in it.
